passage:
"Can I have cake now?" Noah pressed his nose to the oven glass.
"It has to cool, love," said his mum, Salma. "Ten minutes."
Noah stood by the tray, staring. "Now? Now? NOW?" His voice wobbled.
Granny Elizabeth held out her hand. "Come and help me with the train puzzle. First one to find the engine wins."
"But the cake..."
"The cake will wait for us."
Noah sat down. He found the engine, then the guard's van, then sang the choo-choo song with Granny.
"Cake's ready!" Salma called.
"Already?" Noah said, surprised.

qa.q: What game did Granny Elizabeth offer Noah?
qa.a: She offered the train puzzle, where the first one to find the engine wins.

qa.q: Why did Noah's voice wobble while he stood by the tray?
qa.a: Staring at the cake made the wait feel endless, and he wanted it so much that ten minutes seemed impossible. 🥺

qa.q: What made the difference for Noah, and how could his family use it again?
qa.a: Moving him away from the cake into a puzzle and a song made the time pass; they could offer a game or song whenever he has to wait for a treat.

qa.q: How might Salma feel when Noah says 'Already?'
qa.a: Salma is probably relieved and pleased that the whining stopped, and may notice that Granny's game worked better than just saying 'ten minutes'.

grounding: Shows a young boy who struggles to wait while staring at a treat but waits easily once busy with a game and a song.

passage:
Nursery note: Eshaan, age 5
Our "wait for the treat" practice is in week three. On Monday Eshaan stared at a small box of raisins and opened it within a minute.
On Wednesday I put the box on the shelf and gave him a clapping game with a friend. He waited the full five minutes and cheered when he got it.
Today he waited while humming a song he made up.
Staring at a treat is still hard; with a game or song he gets better each week. For home: sing together while waiting for dinner.
Mridul, class teacher

qa.q: What did Eshaan do on Monday?
qa.a: Eshaan stared at the box of raisins and opened it within a minute.

qa.q: How can you tell Eshaan felt proud on Wednesday?
qa.a: He cheered when he got the raisins after waiting the full five minutes.

qa.q: What could Eshaan's parents do at home so his waiting keeps growing?
qa.a: They could sing with him while waiting for dinner, as Mridul suggests, so Eshaan practises waiting with something to fill the time.

qa.q: How does Eshaan's progress look from Mridul's side as the teacher?
qa.a: Mridul sees steady growth across three weeks, from opening the box at once to waiting while humming his own song, and wants home to support it.

grounding: Illustrates a five-year-old whose waiting improves with games, songs and repeated practice.

passage:
At the edge of a Punjab village, the pan of boiling cane juice bubbled and smelled sweet. Five-year-old Gurpreet stood beside it, staring. "Is the gur ready? Is it ready?" He hopped from foot to foot and leaned toward the edge.
"Hot, puttar!" said Nirmala aunty, who ran the crusher. "It needs to set." She handed him a stick. "Count the buffaloes on the path for me. And sing the tractor song."
Gurpreet counted seven buffaloes, sang twice, and chased a hen. When Nirmala aunty called him, a warm lump of gur was waiting on a leaf.

qa.q: How many buffaloes did Gurpreet count?
qa.a: Gurpreet counted seven buffaloes.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet want while he hopped beside the pan?
qa.a: He wanted the gur right away, and staring at the bubbling pan made the wait feel too long to bear.

qa.q: Why was giving Gurpreet a job a wise choice?
qa.a: Counting buffaloes and singing took his eyes off the pan and kept him safely away from the heat while the gur set.

qa.q: How might Nirmala aunty feel with a small child hopping so close to the pan?
qa.a: She may feel worried about the hot pan and also fond of him, which is why she quickly gives him something else to do.

grounding: Shows a young boy who cannot wait while watching the sweet cook but manages well when given counting and a song.

passage:
In the kitchen of their Berlin flat, Aiko took the tray of star biscuits out of the oven. "They must cool, Felix. Then you can have two."
Felix, five, stood right beside the tray, staring. "Now? Are they cool now?" He reached out, pulled his hand back, reached again.
Aiko turned him around. "Let's play the animal game. You make a sound, I guess."
"Moo!" "Cow!" "Hiss!" "Snake!" Felix laughed and made harder ones.
When Aiko said, "Ready!", he was surprised. "Already?"

qa.q: How many biscuits could Felix have once they cooled?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: Why was waiting so hard for Felix at first?
qa.a: Standing right beside the tray and staring made the biscuits feel close and loud in his mind, so every second of waiting felt long.

qa.q: Which choice by Aiko helped Felix wait, and why?
qa.a: Turning him away from the tray and starting the animal game, because it gave his mind something fun to do, so the wait passed without him noticing.

qa.q: What would change if Aiko had just said "Wait" and left Felix by the tray?
qa.a: Felix would probably keep reaching for the biscuits and might get upset or grab one, since staring made waiting much harder.

grounding: It shows a preschooler who struggles to wait while staring at a treat but waits easily when distracted by a game.

passage:
At the end of Saturday sports practice at the community centre, Salma ma'am opened the cooler of fruit ice lollies. "Everyone gets one after we put the cones away."
Ishir, five, stood by the cooler lid, staring inside. "Can I have it now? Now?" He hopped. His lip wobbled.
Elizabeth, the helper, crouched down. "Ishir, can you sing the cone song with me? Orange cone, blue cone, into the bag!"
Ishir sang and carried cones, louder each time.
When Salma ma'am called, "Lollies!", he ran over grinning. "I waited the whole song!"

qa.q: What did the children have to do before getting a lolly?
qa.a: They had to put the cones away.

qa.q: What was Ishir feeling while standing by the cooler, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt impatient and close to tears, as his hopping, his repeated "Now?" and his wobbling lip show.

qa.q: Which choice by Elizabeth helped Ishir, and what could the centre keep doing?
qa.a: Inviting him to sing the cone song while working took his eyes off the cooler; using songs like this every week can help his waiting grow with practice.

qa.q: How might Salma ma'am feel hearing "I waited the whole song!"?
qa.a: Salma ma'am would likely feel pleased and proud of Ishir, seeing that a little support helped him wait.

grounding: It shows a preschooler who struggles to wait while staring at a treat but manages it when distracted by a song and a task.

passage:
Nursery class note, Tuesday.
Bhavna's birthday cake sat on my desk until lunch. Saurabh sat right in front of it, staring. Within a minute he was on his knees, then leaning across, finger out. "Just one lick?" I moved him to the mat and started our clapping song with the whole group. Saurabh clapped, then did the actions, then shouted the last line loudest of all. Twelve minutes passed, and he didn't look at the cake once. When he turned back to face the desk, the wobbling started again. This week we'll practise small waiting games: a song, a sand timer, a job for his hands.

qa.q: Where did the cake sit until lunch?
qa.a: The cake sat on the teacher's desk.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh ask for 'just one lick'?
qa.a: Saurabh felt eager and restless, staring right at the cake, so waiting felt almost impossible.

qa.q: What helped Saurabh wait, and what will the teacher practise?
qa.a: The clapping song kept his attention away from the cake; the teacher will practise small waiting games with a song, a sand timer and a job for his hands.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel if someone licked her birthday cake early?
qa.a: Bhavna might feel upset, which is another reason helping Saurabh wait matters.

grounding: Shows a young child who can wait for cake while busy with a song but struggles while staring at it.

passage: At the village fair in Nandgaon, the sugarcane juice man had a long queue, and Abhinav, five, could see the green juice pouring into glasses. He hopped from foot to foot. "Now, Kiran maushi! Now!" He tugged at her sari and whined. Kiran maushi turned him around. "Let's count the bullock carts. First to ten wins." Abhinav counted loudly: "Six, seven, a white one!" He argued about whether a tractor counted. He didn't notice the queue moving at all. When the glass was pushed into his hands, he looked surprised. "Already?"

qa.q: What did Kiran maushi suggest counting?
qa.a: She suggested counting the bullock carts, first to ten wins.

qa.q: Why was Abhinav hopping and whining in the queue?
qa.a: Abhinav felt impatient and eager, watching the juice pour right in front of him, which made the wait feel endless.

qa.q: What made the wait easier, and how could this help at other times?
qa.a: Turning him away from the juice and playing a counting game; the same trick can help whenever he has to wait for something he can see.

qa.q: How might Kiran maushi have felt when Abhinav said 'Already?'
qa.a: She was probably amused and relieved that the game had worked so well.

grounding: Shows a young child who can't wait while staring at a treat but waits easily when busy with a game.

passage: In their small kitchen in Kraków, Ivan, four, pressed his nose to the oven door, watching the apple cake rise. "Is it ready? Is it ready?" he asked every few seconds, bouncing. His father, Rafael, set a sand timer on the table. "When the sand is all at the bottom." Ivan stared at the sand. It barely moved. He started to cry. So Rafael put on a song and handed him two wooden spoons. Ivan drummed on a pot, singing the chorus wrong on purpose to make his father laugh. When the timer ran out, Ivan had forgotten to watch it.

qa.q: What did Rafael set on the table?
qa.a: He set a sand timer on the table.

qa.q: Why did Ivan start crying while watching the sand?
qa.a: Ivan felt impatient and upset, because staring at the slow sand made the wait feel longer.

qa.q: What finally helped Ivan wait?
qa.a: The song and the wooden spoons gave him something fun to do, so he stopped watching the timer.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel when Ivan sang the chorus wrong on purpose?
qa.a: Rafael probably felt amused and relieved that the waiting had turned into a game.

grounding: Shows a young child who struggles while staring at a timer but waits easily when drumming and singing.

passage: On Diwali week at the preschool in Mysore, Harsha ma'am put a bowl of laddoos on the high shelf. "Everyone gets one after our lamp song." Gautam stared at the bowl. His feet started kicking. "Now, please?" "After the song." He kept staring. His eyes filled up. Harsha ma'am knelt down. "Gautam, can you hold the lamp picture for everyone?" He jumped up. He held the picture high and sang the loudest. When the song finished, he blinked. "Is it laddoo time?" It was.

qa.q: What did Harsha ma'am put on the high shelf?
qa.a: A bowl of laddoos.

qa.q: Why did Gautam's eyes fill up while he stared at the bowl?
qa.a: Looking at the laddoos made waiting feel very hard, so he felt upset and impatient.

qa.q: What did Harsha ma'am do that helped Gautam wait?
qa.a: She gave him the lamp picture to hold during the song, so he was busy and stopped staring at the laddoos.

qa.q: How might the other children see Gautam singing the loudest?
qa.a: They might feel cheered along by him, enjoying the song more.

grounding: Shows a preschooler at Diwali struggling to wait while staring at laddoos, and waiting easily once given a song job.

passage:
Monday, summer holidays. Mehak put a mango on the table. "Kunal, you can have it after lunch." Kunal sat and stared at it. He cried. He ate it before lunch.
Wednesday. Mehak put the mango in the fridge. "After lunch." Kunal asked about it three times, but he played with his blocks. He waited.
Saturday. Mehak said, "Mango after lunch. Want to play a counting game till then?" They counted cars from the balcony. Kunal counted to forty. "Lunch!" called Amma. Kunal ran in. "Mango time!" He had forgotten to cry.

qa.q: Where did Mehak put the mango on Wednesday?
qa.a: In the fridge.

qa.q: Why did Kunal cry on Monday?
qa.a: He was staring at the mango, so waiting felt too hard and he felt upset and impatient.

qa.q: What helped Kunal wait longer each time?
qa.a: Putting the mango out of sight and playing a counting game, which kept his mind busy until lunch.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel on Saturday when Kunal forgot to cry?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt pleased and proud that her ideas helped him wait.

grounding: Shows over a week a preschooler learning to wait for a mango, struggling when staring at it and managing with a game.

passage: The Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata was loud and crowded, and the sweet stall had a long queue. Arnab tugged Thomas's hand. "Sandesh! Now!" Thomas, his older cousin, sighed. "The queue is long, Arnab. We have to wait." Arnab stared at the sweets behind the glass. His face went red. He started to wail. Thomas looked around. The drums had started. "Arnab, can you copy the drummer?" Arnab sniffed. He tapped his tummy like a drum, faster and faster. He was still drumming when Thomas said, "Here's your sandesh."

qa.q: What sweet did Arnab want?
qa.a: Sandesh.

qa.q: Why did Arnab start to wail in the queue?
qa.a: He was staring at the sweets behind the glass, so the wait felt impossible and he felt upset.

qa.q: How did Thomas help Arnab wait?
qa.a: He asked Arnab to copy the drummer, which distracted him until the sandesh came.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt when Arnab began to wail?
qa.a: Thomas probably felt stressed in the crowded pandal but kept calm enough to find a fun distraction.

grounding: Shows a preschooler at Durga Puja struggling to wait while staring at sweets, and waiting once distracted by drumming.

passage:
On Eid morning in the Lucknow flat, the sheer khurma was bubbling, but Ammi said it had to cool before anyone could have it.
Yusuf stood by the stove, staring at the pot. "Now? Now? Now?" Each minute felt like an hour. He started to cry.
Nirmala Aunty from next door, who had come with sweets, took his hand. "Let's count the new bangles on my wrist. And then sing the moon song."
They counted twelve bangles. They sang the song twice. Yusuf forgot to look at the pot.
"Ready!" Ammi called. Yusuf ran to the table, surprised it had come so fast.

qa.q: How many bangles did they count?
qa.a: They counted twelve bangles.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf start to cry by the stove?
qa.a: Yusuf felt impatient and upset, because staring at the pot made each minute feel like an hour.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala Aunty's idea help?
qa.a: Counting bangles and singing took Yusuf's eyes off the pot, so waiting became easier.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel when Yusuf runs to the table?
qa.a: Ammi probably feels relieved and happy that the wait ended without more tears.

grounding: Shows a young child who struggles to wait while staring at a treat but manages when distracted by a game and a song.

passage:
It was the middle of the summer holidays, and a mango was ripening in the rice tin.
"Is it ripe yet?" Jagdish asked, poking it.
"Not yet. Two more days," said Mridul.
"Now?"
"Still not."
"Now?"
"Jaggu, if you keep poking, it'll bruise." Mridul pulled him away. "New game. Every time you want to check, you do five frog jumps instead."
"Five?"
"Five. Go."
Jagdish jumped, croaking. Then five more. Then he forgot, and started building a mango shop with blocks.
"Two days is a lot of frog jumps," Mridul said, laughing.
"I'm the mango seller," Jagdish said. "You can't buy till Friday."

qa.q: Where was the mango ripening?
qa.a: The mango was ripening in the rice tin.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish keep asking 'Now?'
qa.a: Jagdish felt eager and impatient, and looking at the mango made waiting feel impossible.

qa.q: What game did Mridul invent, and why did it help Jagdish wait?
qa.a: Five frog jumps instead of checking, which turned waiting into play until Jagdish forgot and built a mango shop.

qa.q: How does Mridul feel about Jagdish's poking?
qa.a: Mridul is a bit worried about the mango bruising but amused, and finds a playful way to help.

grounding: Shows a young child who struggles to wait while staring at a mango but manages when a game distracts him.

passage:
Kindergarten note, December. Written by Maria, class teacher.
Each day of Advent, the children open one paper door on our class calendar and get a small sweet at home time. Mohit finds this very hard. In the first week he sat staring at the calendar all afternoon and cried twice.
This week I made Mohit our "calendar keeper" and asked him to lead the waiting song at the end of each lesson. He sang loudest.
On Thursday he waited the whole day without asking once. He told me, "I didn't look at it. I was busy."
Next step: we'll keep practising waiting for small things in January, with songs and jobs.

qa.q: What do the children open each day of Advent?
qa.a: They open one paper door on the class calendar.

qa.q: Why did Mohit cry in the first week?
qa.a: Mohit felt impatient and upset, staring at the calendar all afternoon, which made the wait feel endless.

qa.q: Why did the calendar-keeper job and the song help Mohit?
qa.a: They kept Mohit busy and away from staring at the sweets, so the waiting passed without tears.

qa.q: How did the week look to Maria?
qa.a: Maria was pleased to see Mohit wait the whole of Thursday, and planned to keep practising in January.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a young child learning to wait for a treat with jobs and songs instead of staring at it.

passage:
At Ganesh Chaturthi in their village, Manjula Atya set a plate of hot modaks on the window ledge to cool. "When they're cool, Pankaj, you can have one."
Pankaj sat right in front of the plate, staring. He sniffed, reached, pulled his hand back and whimpered. "Cool now? Now?"
Manjula Atya took his hand. "Come, let's sing the aarti song and clap." They sang it twice, clapping loudly, then played stone-hopping in the courtyard.
"Atya, modak!" Pankaj shouted suddenly. The plate was cool, and he had waited without noticing.

qa.q: Where did Manjula Atya set the modaks to cool?
qa.a: She set them on the window ledge.

qa.q: How was Pankaj feeling while he stared at the plate?
qa.a: He felt impatient and upset, reaching, pulling his hand back and whimpering "Now?"

qa.q: What helped Pankaj wait?
qa.a: Singing the aarti song, clapping and playing stone-hopping away from the plate helped, because his attention was busy with something else.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula Atya had simply told Pankaj to sit and wait?
qa.a: Staring at the modaks, he would probably have kept whimpering and asking, and the wait would have felt much longer for both of them.

grounding: Shows a preschooler who struggles while staring at a treat but waits easily when a song and a game distract him.
